blocks.text: Start almost every liver question with ultrasound (US) and Doppler: no radiation, no sedation, done at the bedside. Add magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) when ultrasound cannot answer. Use computed tomography (CT) rarely: abdominal CT is the highest-dose pediatric scan.

blocks.h: After liver transplant: hepatic artery thrombosis
blocks.text: Hepatic artery thrombosis (HAT) affected 7.4% of first pediatric transplants within 90 days (Ebel 2020). No arterial signal, or a new tardus parvus waveform with rising enzymes: call the transplant surgeon now. Do not let more imaging delay re-exploration (expert practice). Tardus parvus is a screen, not a diagnosis.

blocks.h: A normal ultrasound does not exclude biliary atresia
blocks.text: NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN 2017: a normal scan does not rule out non-syndromic atresia. Pale stools or a rising GGT: go on to biopsy or cholangiogram without delay. If the first scan is normal and stools stay pale, scan again.

blocks.h: Infant cholestasis ultrasound: what to ask for

sub: Fast 4 hours: a fed gallbladder contracts and looks abnormal.
Do not fast a hypoglycemic or hypopituitary infant: scan non-fasting.
High-frequency linear probe and an operator looking for atresia on purpose.
Length, wall, lining and contour.
Contraction after a feed.
Triangular cord: echogenic plate anterior to the right portal vein.
Cyst at the hilum and whether intrahepatic ducts are dilated.
Hepatic artery diameter.
Subcapsular flow along the liver surface.
Polysplenia, situs, preduodenal portal vein, interrupted inferior vena cava (IVC).
If present: echocardiogram and tell the surgeon.

head: Sign
Definition
Sensitivity / specificity
rows: Length < 1.9 cm, irregular contour, no smooth echogenic lining
Echogenic plate > 4 mm anterior to the right portal vein
Color flow along the liver surface
Right hepatic artery > 1.5 mm at the porta

blocks.text: A positive sign is actionable: proceed to biopsy or cholangiogram. A negative sign changes nothing. Doppler signs are the most sensitive: use them to look harder, not to decide. Pooled data: Zhou 2016 (23 studies); single centers: Lee 2009 (subcapsular flow, n = 64), Kim 2007 (hepatic artery, n = 68).

blocks.h: HIDA and infant MRCP: rule-out tests only

sub: Excretion into the bowel argues strongly against atresia.

Non-excretion is non-specific: neonatal hepatitis and bile duct paucity fail to excrete too (Gilmour 1997); NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN 2017 add PiZZ alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, low birth weight and parenteral nutrition (PN).
Pooled sensitivity 98.7%, specificity 70.4% (Kianifar 2013, 81 studies).
Phenobarbital premedication takes 3–5 days and changed nothing in the only randomized trial (Malik 2015): never let it delay biopsy or cholangiogram.
Seeing the whole extrahepatic tree excludes atresia; not seeing it proves nothing.
Sensitivity 96%, specificity 58% (Wang 2018, 5 studies).
The infant duct is about 1 mm and collapsed: partial volume hides it.
The only test high on both axes: sensitivity 98%, specificity 93% (Wang 2018, 11 studies).

blocks.h: Spleen length: upper limit by age
head: Age
Upper limit

blocks.text: Coronal length through the hilum, quiet breathing (Rosenberg 1991, 230 children). For a short child with chronic disease, height- and weight-based limits fit better (Megremis 2004). The platelet : spleen-length z-score ratio predicts varices (area under the curve 0.84; Gana 2011): use it to prioritize endoscopy, not to skip it.

blocks.h: Pediatric Doppler is not adult Doppler
items: Spleen: use age limits, not the adult 13 cm.
Portal vein pulsatility in a child with liver disease suggests portal hypertension, not right-heart disease (Westra 1995).
Cavernoma with a patent left portal vein in the Rex recess: refer for MesoRex bypass (Baveno VI pediatric 2016).
Before transplant in atresia: portal vein ≤ 4 mm or hepatofugal flow predicted early portal vein thrombosis (Gu 2015). Report diameter and direction to the surgeon.

After transplant, read velocities against day-specific pediatric ranges (Verhagen 2023): the hepatic artery stays well below the adult 200 cm/s cutoff; the portal vein exceeds the adult 125 cm/s in the first days, then its normal range falls to about 60 cm/s by 1 year — a late stenosis can look normal by adult rules.
Hepatic artery resistive index ≥ 1.0 in biliary atresia predicted early death in one center: expedite transplant evaluation (Broide 1997; not validated elsewhere).
Abdominal CT: 14–25% of pediatric abdomen/pelvis scans gave ≥ 20 mSv (Miglioretti 2013).
If CT is needed: child-size protocol, one phase.
MRI under about 4 months: feed-and-wrap often avoids sedation (Lollert 2024).
Book an MRCP only if the answer will change the plan.

items.text: Gallbladder ghost triad: 30 of 31 infants with atresia, no false positives. The 31st had a normal gallbladder at 6 weeks and a ghost at 8 (Tan Kendrick 2003).
A thick gallbladder wall argues for hepatitis, not atresia: seen in 46 of 186 infants without atresia and in none with it (Tan Kendrick 2003).
Non-excreting HIDA is not atresia: 13 of 53 non-excreting infants had neonatal hepatitis, bile duct paucity or PN cholestasis. No infant with atresia excreted (Gilmour 1997).
Normal platelets do not exclude varices. Noninvasive scores triage endoscopy; they do not replace it.
Gadoxetate MRI cannot prove bile duct patency in a cholestatic infant: liver uptake falls when bilirubin is high.
MRI-PDFF grades liver fat in children against biopsy (Middleton 2018). CT attenuation is not the way to measure it.
A 9 cm spleen is normal at 10 years and massive at 3 months.

positions.naspghan_espghan_2017_nc: Selective use: excretion argues against atresia

rows.note: Both agree non-excretion proves nothing. The app treats HIDA as optional and never lets it delay biopsy or cholangiogram.

positions.naspghan_espghan_2017_nc: Liver biopsy; ERCP or percutaneous cholangiography have a limited role
positions.espr_2021_ba_imaging: Percutaneous cholecysto-cholangiography or ERCP, with liver biopsy

rows.note: Use what your center does well. The decision to operate comes from biopsy or a cholangiogram, not from cross-sectional imaging.
Both are adult-led documents. In children, MRCP had 81% sensitivity against ERCP (Ferrara 2002, n = 21): a normal MRCP does not exclude PSC. Keep ERCP for brushing, dilating or stenting a stricture.
